description: I'm CS student, I'm developing a simple health app that uses python to process both (simulated) sensor data and the astronauts own inputs and verify whether they are with any metric indicative of an health issue, and displaying it in an approachable way using react.
summary:
AstraSalus is a gloved-friendly, autonomous crew health monitoring web application built with React, Vite, Python (FastAPI), SQLite, and Pillow. Across long-duration orbital, deep-space transit, lunar, and Martian missions, Earth communication latency and spaceflight hazards—radiation, altered gravity, isolation, and closed-habitat air—require non-physician astronauts to assess and stabilize health issues independently.

AstraSalus tracks 17 physiological and habitat metrics across seven body systems, supporting full check-ins, single-metric partial updates, live webcam or file-based ultrasound, ocular, and skin screening, and interactive trend charts. Using screening thresholds adapted from NASA-STD-3001, it flags syndrome patterns (such as SANS fluid shifts and elevated cabin CO₂), monitors per-exam overdue reminders, and links alerts directly to focused single-issue countermeasures and post-care re-checks, reinforced by non-clinical routine tracking and XP progression.
details:
What AstraSalus Does & How It Works

AstraSalus is a self-contained spacecraft crew health monitoring web application composed of a React HUD frontend and a Python FastAPI backend backed by local SQLite storage and Pillow image analysis.

  1. Mission & Habitat Context: A persistent top bar displays 24-hour MET (Mission Elapsed Time) and UTC clocks, Earth communication latency (AOS), telemetry freshness (>24h stale warning), prioritized Warning/Caution/Advisory counts, overdue exam chips, and an isolated Flight vs. Simulation Mode switcher. Crew can switch between four operational environments—Orbital Space Station (0g LEO), Deep-Space Transit Habitat (0g, 1–20 min lag), Lunar Surface Base (0.16g, ~1.3 s lag), and Mars Rover & Surface Habitat (0.38g, 4–22 min lag)—which dynamically adjust radiation limits (<1.3 vs. <0.9 mSv/day), regolith dust caps (<0.3 vs. <0.1 mg/m³), and autonomous-care escalation guidance.
  2. Multi-Modal Telemetry & Visual Screening: Astronauts can log a full 17-metric check-in with live clinical preview, update individual vitals cleanly via partial telemetry stamps (supporting continuous decimal values such as 98.3% SpO₂ without overwriting unrelated metrics), or record measurements directly inside guided Self-Exam step pages. In the Imaging tab, crew can capture live frames from onboard/USB webcams, upload .png/.jpg/.webp images, or run 1-click synthetic test scans across three modalities (Portable Ultrasound, Ocular/Fundus, and Skin/Wound Camera) analyzed locally by Pillow for luminance, contrast, erythema redness index, and edge texture.
  3. Clinical Engine & Closed-Loop Countermeasures: Every reading is evaluated across 7 body systems (Neurological/Sleep, Ocular/SANS, Cardiovascular, Respiratory/Immune, Metabolic/Hydration, Musculoskeletal, and Skin/Radiation) plus 6 cross-metric syndrome patterns (SANS fluid shifts, CO₂-linked sleep/fatigue, orthostatic depletion, infection/immune, glycemic imbalance, and radiation spikes). When a metric enters Caution or Warning, targeted countermeasures appear directly inside the triage banner and Alerts queue, routing to 14 single-issue countermeasure pages paired with a Post-Countermeasure Re-check shortcut back to the exam.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Enables non-physician crewmembers to perform accurate preventive exams and acute stabilization even during 4–22 minute Mars communication blackouts or latency windows.
  • Prevents missed or conflated checks through independent per-metric cadence reminders (for example, completing intraocular tonometry does not falsely mark the visual acuity screen complete).
  • Supports longitudinal health awareness via interactive 10-day SVG trend charts with nominal operational bands, zoom toggles, and mission-day clinical notes, while encouraging daily adherence through non-clinical routine tracking, streaks, and badges.

Tools, Languages, Software & Hardware Used

  • Frontend: React 19, Vite, JavaScript, CSS, Lucide icons, browser WebRTC (MediaDevices API) & HTML5 Canvas webcam capture, and localStorage checklist persistence.
  • Backend & Data: Python 3.14, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, Pillow (PIL), SQLite, uv, and Ruff.
  • Testing & Documentation: Python unittest (9 backend unit/end-to-end handler tests), ESLint, Vite production build, Git/GitHub, and Typst (for the 7-slide demo PDF).
  • Hardware Used: Windows development PC and integrated/USB webcam for live camera frame capture verification.

Creativity & Key Human-Factors Considerations

  • Gloved Spacecraft Ergonomics: UI targets are sized for 44–50px gloved touch/click operation, separating Health Data, Exam & Care Steps, Alerts, Trends, Self-Check, Imaging, and Routine into uncluttered tabs rather than forcing long vertical scrolling.
  • Single-Issue Protocol Separation: Instead of grouping unrelated advice together, each exam (12 subpages) and preventive/treatment protocol (14 subpages) lives on its own focused page so a low-mood alert routes strictly to behavioral stress tools without mixing unrelated sleep protocols.
  • Safe Non-Clinical Gamification & Simulation Isolation: Progression ranks intentionally avoid medical titles (such as Doctor or Medic) so gamified adherence never implies clinical qualification, and Simulation Mode drills run in isolation from real Flight Mode logs, streaks, and overdue exam timers, with confirmation modals guarding irreversible resets.
  • Reference Standards & Disclosures: Quantitative limits and display rules (Nominal/Caution/Warning colors, directional ↑/↓ arrows, MET/UTC formatting, alert prioritization) draw from public NASA-STD-3001 Vol 1 and Vol 2 (Appendix F) technical specifications. All code, baseline 10-day telemetry trajectories, sample images, and descriptive text acknowledge SI (Synthetic/Artificial Intelligence) generation and contain no NASA branding, logos, flags, or mission identifiers.
